title: Decoder Sparsity in the Neuron Basis
takeaway: In an outside replication, 92% of the learned feature directions turn out to be spread across many MLP neurons rather than concentrated in one neuron or ten. The scatter plot sorts every feature by how much of its decoder vector's squared length sits in its single largest neuron and in the next nine. The sentence attached to it adds a claim the plot itself does not display: that kurtosis still shows the neuron basis is privileged.
walkthrough:
This is the one figure in the paper's [[external-replication]] section, where an invited outside researcher trained his own [[sparse-autoencoder]] on a different open-source one-layer transformer and reported what he got. It is commentary appended to the paper, not one of the authors' own results.

He asks a narrow question. When a learned feature writes into the MLP layer, does it write through a handful of neurons, or through nearly all of them?

### How the axes are built

Each point is one feature from his dictionary. Take that feature's column of the [[dictionary-decoder]] — its [[feature-direction]] — and square every entry. Each neuron now holds a non-negative share of the direction's squared length. Sort the shares and divide by their total.

The x-axis, *Frac Explained by Top Neuron*, is the largest single share. The y-axis, *Frac Explained by Next 9 Neurons*, is the shares ranked 2 through 10 added up. So $x + y$ is how much of the direction lives in its ten biggest neurons.

Two mechanical facts help you read it. Both are fractions of the same total, so $x + y \le 1$. And no neuron in the next nine can beat the top one, so $y \le 9x$. That inequality is the straight diagonal edge slicing the upper-left of the blue cloud; nothing can sit above it.

Colour is a label he assigned: *1-sparse* (red) for features whose top neuron alone explains most of the direction, *10-sparse* (green) for those needing the top ten, *dense* (blue) for the rest. The cutoffs are not printed. The histograms on the top and right edges are the marginal distributions of $x$ and $y$, split by the same three labels.

### What it shows

Blue swamps everything. He reports 4% 1-sparse, 4% 10-sparse, 92% dense, and says he finds this surprising. Features are not neurons wearing a different name — the bulk version of the paper's own case-by-case finding about [[neuron-basis-coefficients]] and [[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis]].

The attached sentence then hedges the other way, and note that the plot does not show it: he says kurtosis — heavy-tailedness of the decoder weights measured in the neuron basis, versus randomly rotated bases — still comes out high. That is the [[kurtosis-privileged-basis-test]] for a [[privileged-basis]]. Heavy tails mean a few neuron coordinates are unusually large, which a random rotation would smear out. So the neuron basis is not arbitrary; features just refuse to line up with single neurons, which is what [[superposition]] predicts.

terms.term: Fraction of Squared Decoder Sum Explained by Top Neuron vs Next 9 Neurons
terms.definition: The plot's title. For each learned feature it compares two quantities: how much of the squared length of that feature's decoder vector is carried by its single biggest neuron coordinate, and how much by the next nine.

The x-axis. The squared value of the feature's largest decoder coordinate, divided by the sum of squares of all its coordinates. A value of 0.8 means one neuron holds 80% of the direction's squared length.
The y-axis. The same quantity for the coordinates ranked second through tenth by magnitude, summed. Adding it to the x-value gives the share held by the top ten neurons together.

The total $\sum_j (W_d)_{ji}^2$ over all neurons $j$ for feature $i$ — the squared L2 length of the feature's decoder column. Both axes are shares of this total, which is why they are comparable and why they cannot together exceed 1.

The output matrix $W_d$ of the sparse autoencoder. Its column for feature $i$ is the direction in MLP activation space that the feature writes along when it fires; the paper uses "decoder" and "dictionary" interchangeably.

The coordinate system given by the MLP's individual neurons — the axes you get for free from the architecture. Expressing a feature direction in this basis is what produces the per-neuron shares plotted here.

The legend title. It names the three-way classification the commenter applied to each feature according to how concentrated its decoder vector is in the neuron basis. The plotting library's raw column name, printed as-is.
Legend entry, red. Features whose decoder direction is well explained by a single neuron — points far to the right and low on the y-axis. He reports 4% of features fall here.
Legend entry, green. Features well explained by their top ten neurons but not by the top one alone — the top neuron carries some but the next nine carry a comparable amount. Also 4% of features.

Legend entry, blue. Features whose direction is spread across far more than ten neurons, so neither the top neuron nor the top ten account for much. The remaining 92%, and visibly the bulk of the points.

The small bar panels along the top and right edges. The top one is the distribution of x-values, the right one the distribution of y-values, each stacked by sparsity_label. They show how many features sit at each value, which the overplotted scatter cloud hides.

A measure of how heavy-tailed a distribution is. Applied here to decoder weight values expressed in the neuron basis: high kurtosis means a few coordinates are much larger than typical, rather than all coordinates being of similar size.

A basis the architecture itself singles out. The MLP's elementwise activation function acts on neurons one at a time, so the neuron basis is not just an arbitrary rotation of activation space, and features have some tendency to align with it.

The control the kurtosis test compares against. Rotate the activation space by a random orthogonal matrix and recompute the weight distribution; if the neuron basis were nothing special, its kurtosis would look like the rotated ones. Higher kurtosis in the neuron basis is the evidence that it is special.
One hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder, treated as a candidate interpretable direction in the model's MLP activation space. Each dot in the scatter is one such unit.

The one-hidden-layer autoencoder with a wide ReLU hidden layer and an L1 penalty on that layer, trained to reconstruct MLP activations. The commenter trained his own on a different model rather than reusing the paper's.

The open-source subject model the commenter used, distinct from the two one-layer transformers ("A" and "B") the paper itself trains. Because the model differs, the numbers here corroborate the paper's qualitative claim rather than reproducing its exact figures.
The paper's section 8, where invited external researchers who had seen preliminary results contribute their own commentary. This figure sits there, not in the main results.

numbers.meaning: Share of the commenter's learned features labelled dense — neither one neuron nor ten neurons explains their decoder direction. He calls this surprising, since it means the overwhelming majority of features are spread thin across the neuron basis.
Share of features well explained by a single neuron. These are the red points at high x. It is the fraction of features that are, in effect, just neurons.
Share of features well explained by neurons 2 through 10 together but not by the top one — the green points. Adding all three labels gives 4 + 4 + 92 = 100%.
The number of neurons on the x-axis: the single largest coordinate. It is 1 because the sharpest test of "this feature is a neuron" is whether one coordinate alone carries the direction.

The number of neurons on the y-axis (ranks 2 through 10). It is also the slope of the hard upper bound $y \le 9x$: nine coordinates each no larger than the top one cannot together exceed nine times it. That bound is the straight diagonal edge on the upper-left of the blue cloud.
The top-ten cutoff, $x + y$. Chosen as a loose threshold for "a small handful of neurons" — sparse enough that a human could still read the feature off a short list of neurons.

The x-axis gridline labels, running from no concentration to almost total concentration in one neuron. Points reach roughly 0.9 at the far right, where a single neuron holds nearly the whole direction.
The y-axis gridline labels. The top of the visible range is around 0.67, so no feature has its next-nine neurons carrying much more than two thirds of the squared length.
Both axes are fractions of the same squared total, so $x + y \le 1$ for every point. This is why no dot appears in the far upper-right corner.

Where the dense features sit. A typical dense feature has its top neuron holding a few percent of the squared length and its next nine holding perhaps 15% — so about a fifth of the direction is in its top ten neurons, and four fifths is spread over everything else.
Where the 1-sparse features sit. A high x with a low y is the signature of one dominant neuron with no close runners-up: the feature really is close to a single neuron.
Where the 10-sparse features sit — a broad band sloping down from upper-left to lower-right, because as the top neuron takes more, less is left for the next nine.

The reference value the dense cloud should be compared against. If a direction were spread perfectly evenly over $n$ MLP neurons, the top neuron would hold $1/n$ of the squared length and the next nine would hold $9/n$. For a model with hundreds or thousands of neurons that is a fraction of a percent, well below where the blue cloud actually sits — so even the dense features are more concentrated than a uniform spread, which is the direction the kurtosis claim points.
